As we drove along , I momentarily fell asleep as a result of the cool weather . Apparently , my driver had missed his way again because he refused to wake me up . <p> As I opened my eyes , I saw a sign that indicated that we were in Oloibiri , that notable community where the oil that fuels our national economy was first discovered in a commercial quantity many years ago . The picture clicked instantly . Thereafter , we saw a construction site that the villagers said was an oil museum project undertaken by the Federal Government . <p> The residents later directed us towards another nearby community known as Otueke , where former President Goodluck Jonathan comes from . We then advanced further to a community called Onuebum before crossing over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the network of creeks , rivers and rivulets as we travelled along , although many of them appeared heavily polluted . <p> The short boat ride provided an opportunity for me to reflect on the potential of the blue economy in Bayelsa State , in particular , and the Niger Delta region . As I spent time thinking about the experience , I wondered why very few conversations are happening on this issue in Nigeria , yet far-reaching innovations are being shaped from the oceans elsewhere in the world . <p> Blue economy is the sustainable use of marine resources for economic growth , job creation and improvement of livelihoods while protecting marine and coastal ecosystems . It encompasses a range of activities , such as fisheries , tourism , offshore energy , shipping , and marine biotechnology , among others . <p> In the Niger Delta , the picture we have about our rivers and oceans is one of disasters , flooding , boat mishaps , kidnapping , piracy , and oil thefts , as though the negatives are all that our blue economy sector can offer . Yet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quantum revenue generated from beneath the surface of our creeks and waterways , from Nembe to Sapele , and from Andoni to Ibeno , and beyond . <p> Despite government efforts and intentions , many Nigerians , including those in the Niger Delta , remain unaware of the potential of the blue economy . <p> Many aspiring professionals have yet to view the ocean as a viable career path . Policymakers still prefer to operate in traditional silos that hamper their productivity and minimise their impact , disconnected from coastal communities . The national policy on marine and blue economy , recently presented by the government , has been applauded as an initial positive step . <p> However , the government alone can not do this . Private sector players , development partners and civil society must come together to bring solutions and adapt examples of best practices . Regional agencies , such as the NDDC and the South-South Development Commission , as well as states and other subnational entities , play a crucial role in coordination and effectiveness . <p> The projected target of generating $ 1.5tn trillion for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The Niger Delta region is best positioned to lead the way . However , a clear roadmap on how this will happen should be articulated as a matter of urgency . <p> The blue economy is central to the future of the Niger Delta region . It will strengthen our economy , lessen the burden of youth unemployment , improve food security and support efforts to adapt to climate change . We need to tell our own story ; otherwise , no one else will . <p> We will no longer allow vested interests to hijack the narratives and twist them in furtherance of their interests and objectives . The enormous potentials that exist should be presented alongside clear pathways to overcome existing challenges . The narrative should be presented in comprehensive yet straightforward language that is accessible to diverse audiences . <p> Researchers must now urgently decouple complex marine knowledge into easy-to-comprehend information . Residents in coastal communities , especially women and youth , should be encouraged to share their stories of experience . <p> That story should not be about risks alone but also about a pragmatic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is our responsibility to amplify these coastal voices to ensure that they are heard in decision-making spaces from boardrooms to parliaments . <p> Strong voices in the region must take control of the conversation with clarity , urgency and purpose . Otherwise , we may lose the chance to uplift our communities again . <p> Our approach in the Niger Delta should now be deliberately different and optimistic . Islands of progress should be encouraged and celebrated in the sea of past disappointments . <p> The last time was during the oil boom , when we pointed fingers elsewhere to external actors far from ourselves . We accused multinational oil companies and the parasitic elite . We have another opportunity , and we can not afford to lose it . This time it will be inexplicable . <p> To make the Niger Delta the expected hub for national blue economy efforts , decisive actions must be taken by relevant stakeholders . Multiple informed sources have confirmed that Nigeria 's over-reliance on the port in Lagos has continued to hinder the country 's maritime potential . Investments in port infrastructure would @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ logistics framework . <p> Revamping more ports in the country will unlock the country 's blue economy . Securing our waterways has become urgent to attract investment in marine transport . <p> Our territorial waters have continued to serve as a haven for unregulated fishing by foreign invaders . @@128926039 <p> The Nigerian government will introduce a new petrol consumption tax starting January 2026 . Under the policy , Nigerians will pay a 5% levy -- equivalent to N500 for every N10,000 spent on petrol . <p> The measure is designed to discourage fossil fuel use and encourage citizens to adopt cleaner energy sources . @@128932441 <h> The Invisible Commodity : Why charcoal is not on Nigeria 's economic map <p> When the federal government announced its plan to unlock $2 billion from Nigeria 's forest economy at the 2025 Forest Economy Summit , it sounded like real progress . The Vice President , Kashim Shettima , stressed the urgency , warning that over 90% of our original forest cover has already been lost . <p> Yet , there 's a contradiction at the heart of this initiative : while advocating a sustainable forest economy , the government is quietly restricting charcoal exports a forest product with huge export potential . It 's like finding treasure but blocking the path to it . We ca n't talk about " trees into trillions " while sidelining the very product tied most directly to them . <p> True , the federal government lifted the charcoal export ban in mid-2023 , but it was n't a full repeal it was conditional . Customs issued Circular No. 8 mandating that all charcoal exports must now carry approval letters from the Ministry of Finance and identification from forest officers at ports @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or if Nigeria misses the EU 's December 2025 deadline for non-deforestation sourcing , risk facing another full ban . In reality , this is n't freedom it 's regulation by exclusion . <p> Charcoal , though often controversial , is more than fuel . It is a biofuel , an export asset , and a source of livelihood for rural communities . In a nation battling climate change , there 's a clear paradox : our forests are shrinking , yet charcoal remains invisible in national policy . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> By refusing to classify it as a formal commodity , Nigeria is missing the chance to regulate its production , establish export frameworks , and set price benchmarks . The result is continued forest loss driven by decades of unsustainable practices and a lack of regulatory structure . <p> We must move from damage control to sustainability . That requires supporting afforestation , reforestation , and policies that recognize forest-based livelihoods rather than erase them . Ignoring these systems means losing more than trees we lose communities , culture , and people . <p> The shift we need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but as assets : managed responsibly , regulated wisely , and integrated into a greener economy that serves everyone , especially the next generation . <p> Charcoal Is Powering Other Economies ; Why Not Ours ? <p> Take Namibia , a country of just 3 million people with a semi-arid landscape . In 2023 , Namibia exported 270,000 tonnes of charcoal worth $80.5 million . Compare that to Nigeria with a far larger population and richer forests which exported only 443 tonnes that same year , valued at just $119,470 . Of this , $54,000 went to the UAE ; the rest trickled into Europe . Let that sink in : a country six times smaller is earning hundreds of times more from one forest product . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> This is n't a production problem it 's a policy failure . Nigeria has greater reserves , stronger climatic advantages , and steady demand from the UAE , EU , and Asia . Yet we do n't regulate , protect , or price the industry . Instead , we allow income to leak away through informal channels and black-market trading @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ few natural exports from Nigeria and charcoal is one of them . But with weak documentation , many shipments remain unrecorded . While our neighbors formalize trade , we let ours operate in disguise . <p> The Invisible Commodity : Why charcoal is not on Nigeria 's economic map <p> Industry research projects the global charcoal market to hit $11.4 billion by 2030 . Nigeria is losing more than 99% of its potential revenue due to the absence of a formal export policy or commodity status for charcoal . <p> This vacuum has ripple effects . Producers face exploitation and underpricing . Government earns no tax revenue from a booming informal export sector . Climate finance and carbon credits are out of reach because the industry is n't tracked . Worst of all , local communities where over 70% of charcoal collectors are women and youth , particularly in the north-central and southwest remain trapped in poverty . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> Towards a Smarter Policy <p> Instead of tightening restrictions , Nigeria should recognize charcoal as a valuable commodity central to its $2 -- 3 billion forest economy agenda . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ land use and non-oil revenue . But unless charcoal is included in that conversation as a registered , regulated , and priced commodity , the effort risks being counterproductive . @@128990029 <p> Nigeria recently achieved legislative and policy breakthroughs in the renewable energy landscape . The 2023 Electricity Act , which abolishes the outdated Electric Power Sector Reform Act of 2005 , has become a landmark energy legislation . This new legislation expands the electricity market in so many ways . It decentralizes power generation , allowing states , Independent Power Producers ( IPPs ) , and individuals to obtain licenses for electricity generation , transmission , and distribution within their respective jurisdictions . The legislation further encourages renewable energy development and utilization through its renewable energy obligations , feed-in tariffs , and the Rural Electrification Fund ( REF ) . Additionally , the Climate Change Act 2021 creates a framework for climate action , including a five-year carbon budget and a National Council on Climate Change . In the policy landscape , Nigeria has also made some great strides . The Energy Transition Plan ( ETP ) was launched in 2022 to foster Nigeria 's net-zero ambition by 2060 . The plan aims to increase renewable energy in electricity generation to 30% by 2030 and 60% by 2060 . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seen real momentum in the energy sector . According to reports , Nigeria signed a $200 million deal with WeLight in March 2025 to deploy mini grids in rural communities . Simultaneously , Nigeria is pushing hard on corporate environmental transparency . According to the International Sustainability Standards Board , businesses will be required to report on their climate and environmental practices under IFRS-aligned disclosure standards by 2027 , with penalties for non-compliance . On the environmental compliance front , NESREA , Nigeria 's environmental enforcement agency , is working to ensure standards are met across energy projects . <p> Where promise falters : Enforcement gaps <p> Although these brushstrokes of reform paint a different picture than Nigeria 's previous struggle with weak regulatory inertia , enforcement gaps still undermine the effective transition to renewables . The national power grid is fragile , unstable , and undermining policy goals . In 2024 alone , the national grid collapsed at least nine times . The World Bank estimates that power failure costs the economy about $29 billion every year . Furthermore , efforts to build 14 utility-scale solar farms , meant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This collapse stemmed from a lack of government guarantees and Nigeria 's risky investment environment . Meanwhile , NESREA remains under-resourced and reactive , rather than proactive . The agency needs technical capacity and stringent penalties for non-compliance . Finally , according to reports , ETP will require an estimated $1.9 trillion to meet its targets by 2060 . Nigeria has not yet mobilized these resources . <p> The way forward <p> As a legal scholar , I have long argued that sustainable development can not be achieved by written laws and policy statements alone . What Nigeria needs is enforceable , transparent , and investor-friendly legal frameworks . To address grid instability , regulators must adopt legal mandates requiring grid operators to integrate renewable energy upgrades , backed by enforceable standards and penalties for repeated system failures . To prevent renewable energy projects from stalling , the government should introduce legally binding investment guarantees and risk-sharing frameworks . This will give investors more confidence that their contracts are secure . To strengthen NESREA 's weak enforcement capacity , the agency should be granted greater funding and mandatory training @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ enforcement officers will be better equipped to evaluate and regulate complex renewable energy projects . To tackle financing gaps , Nigeria should incorporate blended finance into existing energy legislation or new legislation . This would combine public funds , private capital , and climate finance to support renewable energy projects . Compliance lawyers and law firms can also play a vital role in the renewable energy transition . They can structure enforceable agreements that protect both investors and the community interests . Finally , to close the policy implementation gap , Nigeria should establish another centralized monitoring body . This institution must track progress under the ETP and Climate Change Act , publish annual compliance reports , and hold regulators accountable through performance audits . <p> Nigeria now has the legislative tools to drive a clean energy transition . The challenge is turning policy into practice . With strengthened enforcement , strategic legal oversight , and active engagement from compliance lawyers , Nigeria can not only meet its Paris Agreement targets but also unlock economic growth , protect the environment , and deliver reliable energy for millions of Nigerians . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compliance

@@128990108 <h> Why Nigeria needs an effective emission tading scheme <p> Nigeria stands at a critical crossroads in balancing its climate commitments with economic realities . The government 's recent proposal to impose a 5% fuel tax from January 2026 as a way of addressing environmental concerns risks deepening hardship in a country already grappling with inflation , rising energy costs , and widespread poverty . Instead of taxing fuels directly , Nigeria should prioritise strengthening emission regulations and building a robust Emission Trading Scheme ( ETS ) that delivers environmental benefits without worsening the economic burden on ordinary citizens . This is the case in other countries , like Brazil , India , Mexico , Indonesia and Colombia , with comparable economic trajectories like Nigeria . <p> Fuel taxes are often used globally to discourage consumption and fund clean energy transitions . However , in Nigeria , such a policy risks amplifying inequality and pushing many who are on the edge further down . Over 63% of the population is classified as multidimensionally poor , and energy affordability is already one of the most pressing challenges since the removal of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ electricity tariffs . A new tax on fuel would cascade through the economy , increasing transport fares , food prices , and the cost of basic services , pushing millions further into financial distress . <p> This policy may be hinged on Nigeria 's commitment to the Paris Agreement and subsequently the signing into law of the Climate Change Act 2021 by late President Muhammadu Buhari to protect the Nigerian environment , ecosystem and livelihoods from the dangers of climate change and ensure a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Advertisement <p> However , this blanket fuel tax does not differentiate between high and low emitters . The wealthy who consume more fossil fuels can more easily absorb higher costs , while the poorest , who already spend a large share of their income on energy and transportation , are disproportionately punished . This creates a regressive system that undermines public trust in climate policy . <p> The Climate Change Act 2021 also stipulates the establishment of the Emission Trading Scheme , which requires a robust regulatory environment for effectiveness , which the government perhaps considers " hard work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tax route . Strengthened emission regulations through ETS would focus on industries and sectors that are the largest contributors to Nigeria 's carbon footprint , such as oil and gas , power generation , cement , and heavy transport . <p> By tightening monitoring , reporting , and verification of emissions , regulators can hold polluting companies accountable without pushing the burden onto households . It has been an existing provision under the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency ( Amendment ) Act , 2007 ( FERMA Act ) . The new tax laws have simply restated and incorporated this provision for harmonisation and transparency within the broader tax reform framework . <p> Implementation is not immediate : While the new tax laws are expected to take effect in January 2026 , the 5% fuel surcharge will not be implemented automatically . Its commencement requires a specific order from the Minister of Finance , which must be published in the Official Gazette . This measure is intended @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ considered , taking into account current economic conditions . <p> Exemptions : The surcharge will not apply to all fuel products . Other clean and renewable energy products <p> Purpose : The surcharge is designed to create a dedicated , sustainable fund for road infrastructure and maintenance . Lower logistics costs and vehicle maintenance expenses <p> Relationship with subsidy removal savings : The presidency argues that while savings from fuel subsidy removal are significant , they are not sufficient to meet Nigeria 's massive and recurring road infrastructure needs . Fees collected will fund replanting and climate resilience programmes , " the commissioner said . <p> Muhammad-Hashim explained that a digital registry of licensed operators and permits had been created , with each permit carrying a QR code for real-time verification . <p> " Monitoring and Enforcement will be carried out in collaboration with security agencies , local government authorities , traditional institutions , and community forest monitors . @@129213525 <h> Why Fact-Checking Is Essential In Academic Writing <p> In today 's information-driven world , students are constantly exposed to an overwhelming amount of content-ranging from scholarly journals to blogs , social media , and online forums . While this access to knowledge is empowering , it also poses a significant challenge : not everything found online is accurate or credible . This is where fact-checking becomes crucial , particularly in academic writing . Whether students are seeking assignment help birmingham resources , consulting research databases , or collaborating with peers , ensuring the accuracy of information is fundamental for producing quality work . <p> Academic institutions uphold integrity as a cornerstone of scholarship , and failing to verify facts can not only weaken an argument but also risk plagiarism , misinformation , or even academic misconduct . This article explores why fact-checking is essential in academic writing , highlighting best practices , common pitfalls , and ways students can strengthen their work with credible research . <h> The Role of Fact-Checking in Academic Integrity <p> Academic writing is not just about presenting ideas-it 's about supporting them with credible @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or misleading claims . For example , when writing an essay about climate change , citing an outdated or biased source could discredit the argument , even if the structure and grammar are flawless . <h> Why It Matters : <p> Protects credibility -- Students earn the trust of professors and peers when their work is grounded in reliable information . <p> The emphasis on fact-checking goes beyond good practice-it 's tied directly to academic integrity policies . Submitting a paper riddled with errors or unverifiable data can lead to lower grades , failed assignments , or disciplinary actions . This is why developing strong fact-checking habits early in academic life is essential . <h> Common Challenges Students Face in Fact-Checking <p> While students recognise the importance of accuracy , they often face obstacles that make fact-checking difficult . Understanding these challenges is the first step toward overcoming them . <p> Information Overload With millions of sources available online , distinguishing between peer-reviewed research and unreliable websites can be daunting . Without careful evaluation , students risk presenting distorted facts that misrepresent reality . <h> Best Practices for Effective Fact-Checking <p> Fact-checking is more than typing a phrase into Google ; it requires critical thinking and systematic evaluation of sources . Cross-Verify Information <p> Never rely on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it should be supported by multiple credible publications . <h> 4 . @@129284206 <h> Watch it , obesity is dangerous ! <p> UNICEF 's newly released report on increasing obesity among schoolchildren due to fast foods and other unwholesome diets is alarming . <p> Titled ' Feeding Profit : How Food Environments are Failing Children ' , the report warns , " One in 10 children worldwide lives with obesity , and exposure to the marketing of ultra-processed foods is widespread . " <p> Therefore , everybody should be aware of the dangers associated with obesity , a growing lifestyle concern among young people . <p> The report states that obesity surpassed underweight as the more prevalent form of malnutrition in 2025 , affecting 188 million school-aged children and adolescents , and placing them at risk of life-threatening diseases later in life . <p> Drawing data from 190 countries , it notes a decline in the prevalence of underweight among children aged five to 19 in the last 25 years , from nearly 13 per cent to 9.2 per cent . Conversely , obesity is the new threat among schoolchildren all over the world , except in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ countries , where obesity rates are the highest . <p> This affects 38 per cent of five to 19-year-olds in Niue , 37 per cent in the Cook Islands , and 33 per cent in Nauru . <p> Over the last quarter of a century , these populations have recorded a large-scale shift from traditional diets to energy-dense imported foods . <p> Also affected , according to UNICEF , are several high-income countries , with obese five to 19-year-olds accounting for 27 per cent in Chile , 21 per cent in the United States , and 21 per cent in the United Arab Emirates . <p> Although undernutrition remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries , overweight and obesity are expanding concerns among school-aged children . <p> According to the latest available data , one in five children and adolescents aged five to 19 globally -- or 391 million -- are overweight , with a large proportion of them now classified as living with obesity . <p> The problem of obesity in children arises when they are significantly heavier than what is healthy for their age , sex @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ overweight and leads to a higher risk of developing insulin resistance and high blood pressure , as well as life-threatening diseases later in life , including type 2 diabetes , cardiovascular disease , and certain cancers . <p> Obesity results from feeding children ultra-processed and fast foods , which are typically high in sugar , refined starch , salt , unhealthy fats , and additives . <p> It is common for producers of these unwholesome foods to donate them in large quantities to schools as part of their corporate social responsibility . These foods are presented as prizes and refreshments at various competitions and social events involving children . <p> It is concerning that traditional foods are being significantly sidelined as parents claim busy schedules constrain them from spending time preparing well-cooked meals . Beverages laced with various unwholesome ingredients are offloaded to shops , restaurants , and schools . They are now easily accessible in malls and can be ordered through delivery services . <p> Sub-Saharan Africa is still exempt from the growing epidemic because these energy-dense diets are quite expensive . The pervasive poverty in the region , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world , makes it difficult for families to sustain themselves on fast food . <p> Nevertheless , the fast-food culture is gradually creeping into countries such as Nigeria . Producers of such instant foods push their easy preparation as bait , which parents easily fall for . <p> Advertisements for these items flood social and traditional media , with juicy offers touted in sales promotions of products . <p> In South Africa , these producers have formed partnerships worth millions of rands with government agencies to earn tax deductions . <p> They position themselves as stakeholders in the government 's National School Nutrition Programme , whereas the underlying motive , as in other countries around the world , is to maximise profits at the expense of public health . <p> Quality health in children is a non-negotiable requirement for national development . Therefore , Nigeria must avoid the pitfalls of other countries caught in poor nutrition and avoid drifting from traditional foods . <p> The huge funds spent on medical treatments can be channelled into expanding access to wholesome nutrition sourced from traditional diets . Quick-service restaurants also count among viable businesses in many countries due to the instant meals and snacks they offer . <p> So , boarding schools must watch the nutritional content of the meals served to children . <p> According to a global poll of 64,000 young people aged 13-24 from over 170 countries conducted through UNICEF 's U-Report platform last year , 75 per cent of respondents recalled seeing advertisements for sugary drinks , snacks , or fast foods in the previous week , and 60 per cent said the advertisements increased their desire to eat the foods . <p> Indeed , the high @@129284750 <h> Disambiguating jurisdictional boundaries of federal , state governments in electricity regulation <p> The enactment of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria ( CFRN ) , 1999 ( Fifth Alteration ) ( No.17 ) Act , 2023 and the Electricity Act , 2023 which paved way for full devolution of intra-state electricity regulatory powers to state governments have stirred a lot of contestations among stakeholders than ever imagined . <p> The bone of contention appears rooted in the misconception amongst stakeholders regarding the extent of the regulatory powers available to state governments under the current multitier regulatory regime recognised by the CFRN ( Fifth Alteration ) ( No.17 ) Act , 2023 and the EA , 2023 . One of such misconceptions which has gained traction in the media is that the recent constitutional alteration and the consequent enactment of the EA , 2023 have for the first time devolved electricity regulatory powers to sub-nationals to the extent that the newly established State Electricity Regulatory Commissions ( SERCs ) can now regulate ( in all its ramifications ) , electricity generation , transmission and distribution activities within state @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( NERC ) , which hitherto regulated electricity activities nationwide . <p> Relatedly , there are those who are of the strong opinion that under the current legal regime , power plants located within state boundaries should fall under the overriding regulatory powers of SERCs including full takeover and control of the eight ( 8 ) power plants now operated by the eight successor generating companies ( GENCOs ) that emerged after the conclusion of privatization in 2013 . <p> It has also been argued that the EA , 2023 , is an iniquitous and needless piece of legislation which has abolished cross-subsidisation and provided the framework for promotion of energy inequalities especially considering the disproportionate distribution of electricity infrastructure between the northern and southern states of Nigeria . <p> The instant intervention seeks to disambiguate the jurisdictional boundaries of the SERCs and NERC under the current legal regime and shed light on recent debates . <p> To fully understand the jurisdictional confines of the two levels of governments regarding electricity regulation in Nigeria , it must be stated that the Nigerian constitution and the Electricity Act constitute the primary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there are other federal enactments that must be taken into consideration when discussing the regulatory powers of the two levels of government . <p> These include the Standard Organisation of Nigeria ( Establishment ) Act which is the general legislation on national technical standards ; Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission Act which is the general legislation on competition , consumer protection , and anti-trust ; Climate Change Act , 2021 which deals with climate change mitigation and adaptation bearing in mind Nigeria 's international commitment to climate change ; Water Resources Act , CAP W2 , Laws of the Federation of Nigeria ( LFN ) , 2004 which regulates the planning , development and use of water resources that affects more than one state ; National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency ( Establishment ) Act ; and the Environmental Impact Assessment Act , CAP.E12 , LFN , b2004 which are relevant in the area of environmental impact of electricity projects or related activities in the power sector . Additionally , licensed electricity entities operating under the regulatory purview of state regulators are expected to comply with extant federal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ value added tax etc . <p> The above , among others , constitute the gamut of laws that are critical in disambiguating the legislative and regulatory competences of the two levels of government in Nigeria on the issue of electricity and should be well understood by key players in the power sector . <p> With respect to the powers of the two levels of government under the constitution , one must recall that prior to 1999 , the business of electricity generation , transmission and distribution was for decades under the sole control of the defunct National Electric Power Authority ( NEPA ) as a vertically integrated monopoly . <p> The defunct NEPA operated a redial national grid system comprising of on-grid power plants , high voltage transmission lines and distribution lines through which electricity albeit epileptically was supplied to Nigerian nationwide without regard to geographic boundaries of state governments . <p> This integrated high voltage system of interconnected generation plants , transmission lines , substations and related facilities crisscrossing states of the Federation and beyond that was operated by NEPA as a unified network is what is essentially referred @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ following the promulgation of the CFRN , 1999 , electric power was included as an item on the concurrent list . In this regard , item F , paragraphs 13,14 , and 15 , Part II , Second Schedule to the CFRN , 1999 ( " the Constitution " ) defined the legislative competence of the respective levels of government regarding electricity . <p> The implication of the aforementioned constitutional provisions is that , since 1999 , state governments were at liberty to invest in electricity within their domains including the power to set up of state grids and regulate intra-state electricity where they possess the wherewithal . No state government took advantage of this constitutional provision either due to lack of the political will or some other inexplicable reasons . <p> It is , however , important to note that prior to constitutional alteration in 2023 , the powers of State Houses of Assembly to legislate on intra-state electricity generation , transmission and distribution activities was greatly impeded by the restriction under paragraph 14 ( b ) , Part II , Second Schedule to the Constitution " to *areas @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " * . <p> It was this restrictive phrase " *to areas not covered by the national grid system within that State* " that was essentially deleted through the enactment of the CFRN , 1999 ( Fifth Alteration ) ( No.17 ) Act , 2023 . According to the long title to the CFRN , 1999 ( Fifth Alteration ) ( No , 17 ) Act , 2023 , the constitutional alteration was intended to " allow states to generate , transmit and distribute electricity in areas covered by the national grid " .... What is apparent from the foregoing is that it is not correct to say that the CFRN , 1999 , ( Fifth Alteration ) Act ( No.17 ) Act , 2023 for the first time transferred " electric power " from the exclusive list to the concurrent list as it is often reported in some sections of the media . Electric power was an item in the concurrent list to the CFRN 1999 and remains so even after the said constitutional alteration of 2023 . <p> What the CFRN , 1999 ( Fifth Alteration ) ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the inhibitive words " *to areas not covered by the national grid system within that State " * to allow state governments legislate on and regulate intra-state electricity activities and most fundamentally " generate , transmit and distribute electricity in areas covered by the national grid " as expressly stated in the long title . <p> In other words , the constitutional alteration was not aimed at empowering state governments to embark on far reaching regulatory measures that would conflict or undermine the regulatory powers of the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission ( NERC ) such as taking over NERC licensed on-grid power plants , setting tariffs or slashing tariffs for electricity procured through the National Wholesale Electricity Market ( NWEN ) or regulation of other activities on the national grid . <p> The constitutional alteration was primarily intended to promote investments within state boundaries without being inhibited by the presence of the national grid or component of it within such state boundaries . <p> In simple terms , by virtue of this constitutional alteration , state governments can now embark on embedded generation , mini-grids , One @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a compelling framework for addressing energy inequalities is the provision of Section 110 which imposes an obligation on NERC to ensure fair spread of transmission and other electricity infrastructure across the country . Similarly , the EA , 2023 for the first time made provision for integrated resource planning and leveraging on this provision the Federal Executive Council recently approved the National Integrated Electricity Policy and Implementation Plan , 2024 which takes into consideration the peculiar strengths and weaknesses of the various state governments . It is expected that state governments will take advantage of this paradigm shift that recognizes a robust role for wind , biomas , solar and other renewable sources of energy in addressing perceived or existing energy inequalities . <p> From the foregoing , it can be safely concluded that the current legal regime for regulation electricity in Nigeria as articulated above leaves no room for confusion or controversy . Farmers responded by abandoning degraded plots and seeking fertile soils in forests . Inheritance deepened the cycle , as children of cocoa farmers carried on the trade and cleared new ground as families expanded . <p> " The moment farmers see their productivity per hectare drop , they start looking for new areas . @@129328513 <h> Saving the ozone layer <p> Today , Nigeria joins the rest of the global community in celebrating this year 's World Ozone Day . Themed , " From Science to Global Action " this year 's commemoration marks the 40th anniversary of the global effort to save mankind from an imminent doom . <p> In the 1980s and 1990s , the gaping holes in the ozone layer hurled down a scary phenomenon . The gloom was discovered by the scientists precisely in 1985 as the fallout of human activities such as ozone-depleting substances ( ODS ) widely used in refrigeration and air-conditioning aerosols . <p> The ozone layer hangs high up in the atmosphere between 10 and 40 kilometres above the earth surface . The region is called stratosphere and it contains about 90 per cent of all ozone in the atmosphere with the capacity to absorb some of the sun 's biologically harmful ultraviolet radiation . <p> Disturbed by the emerging man-made enemy , policymakers and scientists from around the world scrambled to Montreal , Canada , to hammer out a Protocol which was adopted in 1987 . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ potent global-warming gases was phased out around the world and huge successes were recorded over the ensuing decades . It is believed that over 98 per cent of identified ODS have now been eliminated . Scientists have also predicted that the " healing " might return the ozone layer and the global climate to the 1980 levels by around 2050 if the protocol is not breached , thus averting the catastrophe that may result in over two million cases of skin cancer yearly by 2030 . <p> On December 19 , 1994 , the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed September 16 every year as International Day for the Prevention of the Ozone Layer to commemorate the same date on which the Montreal Protocol on Ozone Depleting Substances ( ODS ) was signed . <p> The protocol which has been substantially ratified between 1990 and 1992 stipulates that the production and consumption of compounds that deplete ozone in the stratosphere are to be phased out in a specified period of time . The ODS are widely used in refrigerators , air-conditioners , in dry cleaning , as solvents for cleaning electronic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ published by the Geophysical Research Letters showed that the Montreal Treaty , using data from the United States ' National Aeronautical and Space Agency ( NASA ) , has recorded 20 per cent success in ozone depletion in the Antarctic since 2005 . However , experts say it would take between 50 and 100 years for the holes to disappear completely if the rules are strictly followed . <p> It is sad to note that the recourse to the usage of hydro-fluorocarbons ( HFCs ) as substitutes for ODS has also been discovered to be more extremely deadly climate-warming gases that can be thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide in contributing to climate change . The new reality triggered off the Kigali Amendment to the Protocol aimed at getting ratifying countries to cut their production and consumption of HFCs by more than 30 per cent over the next three decades . <p> Recent studies have also shown that preserving peat lands is also very necessary not only for keeping carbon dioxide in the ground but also to prevent the emission of nitrous oxide which has turned out to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over the world . <p> Without a doubt , one of the direct consequences of ozone layer depletion is climate change . The effect of this phenomenon has been with us for close to three decades now . This necessitated the first summit on Climate Change in 1992 under the auspices of the United Nations held in Rio de Janeiro , Brazil . More than 160 countries attended the conference which aimed at averting the global catastrophe that the phenomenon portended for humanity . <p> Similar conferences have been held in countries like Denmark and the United States at various times to review and ratify the Rio de Janeiro Protocols as the man-made condition presents frightening challenges to the global community . The race against climate change , however , suffered a terrible setback recently when President Donald Trump of the United States pulled out of the race in his first term , describing the phenomenon as a hoax despite the potent dangers it presented . <p> It is within man 's power to reduce the emissions that are causing climate change and to catalyse a new era of global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Nigeria . Indices of climate change are there for all to see . Desertification and perennial floods ravaging the country are some of the groundswells of the condition . Also , decades of relentless gas flaring in the Niger Delta region , carbon monoxide emissions from vehicles , failure of successive administrations to provide steady electricity supply which has left Nigeria and its industries to rely on generating sets running into millions to power their businesses , mean that the federal government is not doing enough in the global efforts to avert the impending cataclysm . <p> Nigeria 's commemoration of the important day remains a mere ritual unless the government at all levels is committed to the cause of reversing the dangerous trend .

@@129484863 <h> Main navigation <h> The Plight Of The Fulbe In Nigeria , By Babayola M. Toungo <p> The Fulbe in Nigeria , particularly the nomadic Fulbe , are faced with existential challenges all over the country . Numbering an estimated 15 to 20 million people , the Fulbe ( or Fulani ) constitute one of the largest pastoralist groups in West Africa , with roughly 7 -- 8 million residing in Nigeria alone . They are confronted by complex threats that are gradually restricting their operational space and rendering life increasingly difficult and convoluted . According to recent studies , over 70% of Fulbe herders report experiencing violence or theft of livestock in the past five years , while more than 60% have lost access to at least half of their traditional grazing routes . This crisis is compounded by a compromised media , a negligent government , a passive elite from amidst their own kin who have found comfort in urban areas , a ruthless security system , and a judiciary often all too willing to deprive them of their freedom and property . <p> These are people whose @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and opportunists . In 2021 alone , it was estimated that cattle rustling accounted for the loss of over 250,000 heads of cattle across Nigeria , with Fulbe herders disproportionately affected . When faced with loss , the Fulbe are unable to seek redress from the police , with restitution often out of reach . Less than 10% of herders report receiving any form of justice or compensation after incidents of livestock theft . Should they resort to self-help , they risk further victimisation and are frequently compelled to pay for their own freedom . Local courts , in particular , seem to relish cases involving the Fulani nomad , rarely dispensing justice in their favour . <p> Beyond the persistent insecurity , the Fulbe face the daily reality of being denied access to land , grazing passage , and water resources - essential elements for their survival as herders . As of 2024 , over 60% of Nigeria 's officially recognised grazing reserves have been encroached upon or converted to farmland , with only about 3 million hectares of the originally designated 10 million hectares remaining accessible . State @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have increasingly blocked access to traditional grazing routes , watering points , and seasonal migration corridors . These restrictions have not only undermined their livelihoods but have also led to increased tension and conflict with settled communities , as competition for dwindling resources intensifies . The Human Rights Watch has documented a marked increase in farmer-herder clashes , with over 2,500 fatalities reported between 2018 and 2022 , the vast majority involving Fulbe herders . <p> Government policies have tended to favour sedentary agriculture , often at the direct expense of nomadic pastoralism . Programmes designed to promote land titling and enclosure have systematically excluded the Fulbe , leaving them with little recourse as their ancestral routes are fenced off or converted to farmlands . According to the National Livestock Transformation Plan ( NLTP ) , less than 5% of Fulbe herders have benefited from land allocation or support , compared to over 40% of settled farmers . Security forces and vigilantes , sometimes operating under the pretext of combating banditry , have been implicated in harassment , extortion , and even violence against Fulbe herders . In many cases @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lack of accountability and the negative stereotypes perpetuated by mainstream media . <p> The media itself plays a significant role in shaping public perception , frequently portraying the Fulbe in a negative light to a gullible and stressed audience desperate for scapegoats . A 2023 media analysis found that over 65% of news reports on rural conflict in Nigeria depicted Fulbe communities as aggressors , with little attention paid to their grievances or the systemic injustices they face . This narrative is readily exploited by a political class eager to capitalise on ethno-religious divisions . The Fulbe are thus rendered invisible in policy debates and are consistently denied a seat at the table when decisions affecting their lives are made . <p> As their space diminishes , the Fulbe find themselves pushed to the margins - socially , economically , and politically . The lack of representation and advocacy means their voices are seldom heard , while the dominant discourse frames them as outsiders or even threats . In the face of these manifold challenges , the resilience of the Fulbe is remarkable , but their future remains uncertain unless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their rights to land , passage , and water . <p> It is crucial to recognise that the Fulbe are not merely the subjects of negative media portrayal but are often victims of violence themselves . Numerous reports highlight that Fulani communities have suffered significant casualties from targeted attacks , yet these incidents receive scant attention or sympathy in mainstream narratives . Instead , the media frequently casts the Fulbe as aggressors , obscuring the reality that many are bereaved and displaced due to the destruction of their communities and livelihoods . <p> This cycle of victimhood and misrepresentation has profound consequences . Stripped of their cattle - the backbone of their economy - and left with little support or justice , some Fulbe , particularly the youth , have turned to banditry as a desperate response to the collapse of their traditional way of life . The destruction of their economic base and the relentless targeting of their people have left many feeling alienated and pushed into the margins , compounding the challenges they already face in an increasingly hostile environment . <p> Addressing the Fulbe 's predicament requires @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with issues of justice , inclusion , and respect for diversity . Only through inclusive dialogue and genuine commitment to fairness can Nigeria hope to resolve the tensions and ensure a future in which the Fulbe , and all communities , can thrive side by side . <p> The plight of the Fulbe in Nigeria is not merely a contemporary crisis , but the culmination of decades of marginalisation , historical grievances , and shifting socio-political landscapes . The roots of their predicament can be traced back to colonial and post-colonial land reforms which increasingly favoured sedentary populations , institutionalising a bias against nomadic lifestyles . This institutional neglect has been aggravated by present-day policies , economic pressures , and demographic expansion , resulting in the systematic erosion of Fulbe autonomy and cultural heritage . <p> Environmental factors have played a significant role in exacerbating their vulnerability . The encroachment of the Sahel due to desertification , unpredictable rainfall patterns , and climate change have forced many Fulbe herders to migrate further south in search of pasture . This southward movement has brought them into closer contact - and often @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ land and water resources . The lack of effective government mediation mechanisms has allowed these disputes to escalate , sometimes spiralling into protracted cycles of violence and retaliation . <p> Furthermore , the Fulbe 's traditional governance structures and conflict resolution systems have been systematically undermined by external authorities , leaving them ill-equipped to negotiate with state actors or assert their rights within the formal legal system . The introduction of modern land tenure laws has failed to recognise communal grazing rights and seasonal mobility , effectively criminalising aspects of their way of life . This legal disenfranchisement , combined with widespread illiteracy and lack of political representation , has rendered the Fulbe particularly susceptible to exploitation and abuse . <p> On a societal level , deep-seated stereotypes and prejudices against the Fulbe have been perpetuated not only by the media , but also by educational curricula , religious institutions , and political rhetoric . These narratives frame the Fulbe as perpetual outsiders , fuelling suspicion and hostility that have translated into discriminatory practices in everyday life - from exclusion in local markets to denial of social services and healthcare @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to their mobile lifestyle and the absence of nomad-friendly schooling options , perpetuating cycles of poverty and marginalisation . <p> The psychological toll of persistent insecurity and social ostracism can not be understated . Generations of Fulbe have grown up in an atmosphere of fear , mistrust , and uncertainty , which has had profound effects on community cohesion and mental health . Women and children are particularly vulnerable , with reports of gender-based violence , abductions , and trafficking in the wake of displacement . The erosion of traditional support networks and the constant threat of violence has undermined the very fabric of Fulbe society . <p> Despite these formidable challenges , the Fulbe have demonstrated remarkable adaptability and resilience . There are growing grassroots movements among Fulbe communities advocating for their rights , seeking legal recognition , and promoting peaceful coexistence with their neighbours . Some initiatives focus on developing participatory land management systems , integrating traditional knowledge with modern practices , and fostering inter-communal dialogue to address misunderstandings and build trust . <p> Ultimately , resolving the crisis facing the Fulbe requires a holistic approach - one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but also tackles the underlying structural inequities and prejudices that have shaped their experience . This entails meaningful policy reforms , inclusive governance , investment in rural infrastructure , and a concerted effort to challenge the narratives that have long cast the Fulbe as scapegoats . Only then can Nigeria move towards a more just and harmonious society , where the rights and dignity of all its peoples are upheld . <p> SaharaReporters.com is an outstanding , groundbreaking news website that encourages citizen journalists to report ongoing corruption and government malfeasance in Africa . Using photos , text , and video dynamically , the site informs and prompts concerned African citizens and activists globally to act , denouncing officially-sanctioned corruption , the material impoverishment of its citizenry , defilement of the environment , and the callous disregard of the democratic principles enshrined in the constitution .

The dewy atmosphere , characterised by air containing a significant amount of water vapour , creates a moist environment with high humidity , resulting in a sticky or damp feeling on the skin . <p> Everywhere becomes cold . You may not have heavy enough clothes to cover yourself up , or at least protect your chest , which houses your lungs , the primary target . Even at night , you may not have heavy enough blankets to cover yourself up . Worst of all , you may not have a room heater to warm your room , and even if you have one , you may not have electricity to power it . <p> The effect of such on asthma patients is , sadly , enormous . An asthma attack , or flare-up , occurs due to inflammation and narrowing of the airways , leading to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tightness . During an attack , the muscles around the bronchial tubes constrict , the airways swell , and mucus builds up , making it extremely difficult to breathe . The experience a COPD patient goes through is unimaginable , something that a man with a good heart would n't wish on his enemy . Air pollution often accumulates during colder months , further stressing the lungs . Managing COPD is like managing asthma -- only much more challenging , because while the latter is reversible , the former is n't . <p> And so I found myself surrounded by all forms of inhalers -- bronchodilators and steroids alike . @@129546305 <h> Renewable Energy And The Challenges Of Oil-Rich Nations <p> Renewable energy is energy that comes from natural resources that can be replenished over time , such as sunlight , wind , rain , and geother ? mal heat . Unlike fossil fuels , which are finite and contribute to climate change , renewable energy is sustainable and has a lower environ ? mental impact , which qualifies for the concept of green energy technology . <p> Green energy technology , in this case , refers to the use of innovative products , systems , and practices that reduce the envi ? ronmental impact of energy production , con ? sumption , and usage . It encompasses various forms of renewable energy , energy efficiency , and sustainable energy solutions . <p> The global transition to renewable energy , otherwise known as green energy technology , is gaining momentum , driven by concerns about climate change , energy security , and economic diversification . <p> Examples of oil-rich countries with signif ? icant levels of transition to green technology are the Middle East countries like Saudi Ara ? bia , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ambitious targets to increase its renewable energy production , aiming to generate 50% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 . The UAE has invested heavily in renewable energy , particularly solar power , and aims to generate 44% of its electricity from clean energy sources by 2050 . Qatar has launched several renewable energy projects , including a solar power plant , and aims to reduce its carbon footprint by 45% come 2040 . <p> However , many oil-rich nations including Nigeria face unique challenges in embrac ? ing renewable energy . This is simply because these countries have long relied on fossil fuels as a primary source of revenue and economic growth , making it difficult to shift away from their traditional energy sources . Struggles to diversify their economies , often intensified by pressure from non-oil rich developed coun ? tries , make them vulnerable to fluctuations in global oil prices . <p> Transitioning to renewable energy re ? quires significant investments in new in ? dustries , infrastructure , and as the world transitions to renewable energy , oil-rich na ? tions risk losing a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ infrastructure and technology needed to support large-scale renewable energy production . Building new infrastructure and developing expertise in renewable energy technologies requires sig ? nificant investment . This also leads to eco ? nomic instability and social unrest . In some oil-rich nations , the fossil fuel industry is deeply ingrained in the culture and society . Transitioning to renewable energy may re ? quire significant changes in behaviour and mind set . This is deeply concerning . <p> However , despite these challenges , there are enormous opportunities for oil-rich na ? tions in transitioning to renewable energy technology . Investing in renewable energy can help oil-rich nations diversify their econo ? mies and reduce their dependence on a single industry . The renewable energy sector has the potential to create new job opportunities and stimulate economic growth . Transitioning to renewable energy can help reduce green ? house gas emissions and mitigate the impacts of climate changes . Investing in renewable energy can ensure long-term sustainability and energy security for oil-rich nations . <p> The Nigerian government has implement ? ed several policies to promote renewable ener ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Master Plan ( REMP ) , which aims to increase renewable electricity generation from 13% of total electricity generation to 36% by 2030 . National Integrated Electricity Policy ( NIEP ) and Integrated Resources Plan ( IRP ) , seek to accelerate energy transition goals , ensure universal electrification , and promote sustainable energy development . National Committee on Renewable Energy , Energy Efficiency , Innovation and Certifi ? cation ( NCREEIC ) , established to promote renewable energy development , energy ef ? ficiency , and innovation . Energy Transition and Critical Minerals ( ETCM ) Roadmap , aims to position Nigeria as a major player in the global clean energy economy . <p> The transition to renewable energy pres ? ents both challenges and opportunities for oil-rich nations . While there are significant hurdles to overcome , investing in renewable energy can help these countries diversify their economies , create new job opportuni ? ties , and ensure long-term sustainability . As the world continues to transition to renewable energy , oil-rich nations must adapt and inno ? vate to remain competitive and relevant in the global energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ while the quest for green energy technology , champi ? oned mostly by western countries with no sufficient oil and gas resources is gaining traction , African countries ( Nigeria in par ? ticular ) must not be in a hurry to abandon the huge oil and gas reserve within our terri ? tory in preference to green energy technology . As a matter of fact , fossil fuel will remain a dominant and dependable source of energy for the world in the next fifty years to come . Our revenue sources must be strictly and ad ? equately protected . <p> For this reason , we hereby call on more Nigerian entrepreneurs and investors to consider setting up indigenous energy com ? panies in order to explore the enormous op ? portunities in this sector . In order to realise the long-term benefits of social equity and inter-generational collaboration , the AU-EU partnership must , therefore , prioritise youth inclusion in the design and implementation of social safety programmes . <p> In Africa , social safety systems barely cater to some crucial populations such as informal sector workers , digital gig workers , and the youths in conflict-prone communities . Especially in Nigeria , the social protection framework fails to integrate the needs of online freelancers , informal workers , and displaced youths in the implementation of empowerment schemes , emergency cash transfers , and other social safety programmes . Despite occupying a significant portion of the country 's workforce -- a portion believed to be over 80 per cent -- the informal workers in Nigeria barely benefit from the social protection framework . This marginalisation sadly affects northeastern Nigeria , where many youths have been displaced by insecurity . <p> Despite being established with the goal of supporting the country 's vulnerable and poor populations , Nigeria 's National Social Register ( NSR ) has performed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ transparency , and prioritising youth-specific support . NSR employs a vague data collection approach , and due to the absence of community oversight and digital transparency , the NSR has failed to accurately document the vulnerable youths in conflict-prone states such as Zamfara and Borno . This failure makes it difficult for Nigeria 's social safety system to properly identify and respond to the specific needs of numerous vulnerable individuals -- unemployed youths , school dropouts , and displaced persons . While Nigeria grapples with the consequences of improper social safety planning , real-world data indicate a worrisome reality as thousands of youths in northeastern Nigeria have come under great insecurity , thereby depriving them of employment opportunities and educational access . The data appears more worrisome , as there are more than 10 million out-of-school children in the country . Similarly , poverty in Nigeria has become a great challenge , driving numerous youths out of school . <p> The AU-EU partnership has a positive implication for Africa ; it could be the effective platform for integrating the European Union 's best practices in restructuring Africa 's social protection @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for the implementation of youth-inclusive and tech-oriented social safety systems in African countries . The EU 's technological sophistication could be the perfect resource for establishing the data systems that would aid effective documentation of informal workers , displaced youths , and other marginalised populations . <p> Moreover , the AU-EU partnership must prioritise the potential of Africa 's vibrant youth population by acknowledging that young Africans have the capacity to effectively manage electronic registration systems , social safety databases , emergency cash payment systems , and other platforms required for the sustenance of effective social safety nets . Towards revamping social safety nets in the AU-EU partnership , the essence of youth integration should never be a subject of debate -- youth integration is , in fact , the catalyst needed to achieve resilient and impactful AU-EU social safety nets . <p> Abdulkareem O. @@129705051 <h> UN at 80 : Reform or fade into irrelevance <p> Eighty years after its founding , the United Nations stands at a defining moment . Created in 1945 to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war and to foster peace , security , and development , the UN emerged as humanity 's most ambitious experiment in global governance . Yet today , its credibility is under mounting strain . From the wars in Ukraine and Gaza , to the humanitarian crises in Sudan , Yemen , and Myanmar , to the accelerating climate emergency , the UN often appears paralyzed , unable to act decisively when the world needs it most . <p> The very architecture that gave the UN legitimacy after the Second World War has become its greatest liability . The Security Council , meant to safeguard peace , is now a theatre of deadlock . Its five permanent members , China , France , Russia , the United Kingdom , and the United States , hold veto powers that can , and often do , silence the will of the majority . This imbalance was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Gaza , and Syria , where geopolitical rivalries eclipsed humanitarian imperatives . For countries in the Global South , the system entrenches inequality , leaving them marginalized in decisions that affect the entire world . <p> Eighty years later , that house of peace is showing its cracks . At this year 's 80th UN General Assembly in New York , the speeches of African leaders carried a blunt message , reform this institution , or it will wither into irrelevance . The tone was not begging , not diplomatic courtesy . It was direct , even defiant . Nigeria 's Vice President Kashim Shettima reminded the Assembly that when the UN was founded , Nigeria did not exist as a sovereign state . It was a colony of 20 million people , excluded from the tables where decisions about its future were made . Today , Nigeria is a nation of more than 236 million , projected to become the third most populous country on earth . It has been a stabilizing force in West Africa , a consistent peacekeeping partner , and a youthful powerhouse . Yet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . His point was sharp , the UN can only recover its credibility when it reflects the world as it is , not as it was . <p> Kenya 's President William Ruto raised the stakes even higher . Standing at the UNGA podium , he cut through the diplomatic niceties . Africa , he declared , deserves two permanent seats on the Security Council , complete with veto power . This is not a favour to Africa , he said , but a necessity for the UN 's own survival . The world can not keep pretending that a continent of 1.4 billion people , the youngest continent , home to some of the fastest-growing economies , should remain voiceless in the council that spends most of its time debating African crises . " Africa dominates most of the Security Council 's agenda , " Ruto said , " yet we remain the only continent without a permanent seat at the table . " His frustration was palpable , and his warning unmistakable . <p> The gap between the UN 's lofty ideals and its limited impact is widening @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unmet , and trust in multilateralism is varnishing . In Africa , the Lake Chad region remains a flashpoint of terrorism and displacement , yet UN responses are seen as sluggish . In Asia , the plight of the Rohingya people remains unresolved . And globally , the Sustainable Development Goals are far off track , with poverty , inequality , and hunger rising once again . <p> Still , all is not lost . Across its vast system , there are pockets of innovation and resilience . The UN has been instrumental in shaping the Paris Agreement on climate change , advancing the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons , and coordinating global humanitarian aid during the COVID-19 pandemic . Its agencies such as WHO , UNICEF , UNHCR , WFP , and others remain lifelines for millions . These successes , however , highlight the paradox , the UN works best when insulated from geopolitics but falters when political will is required . <p> This crisis of relevance is not happening in a vacuum . The world order is shifting . Finnish President Alexander Stubb said it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and power is moving south and east . Africa , Asia , and Latin America are no longer spectators . They are rising as political , economic , and cultural forces . Demographics alone make this inevitable , frica 's population is booming , and its youth are pushing the boundaries of innovation , trade , and culture . To deny such regions a seat at the table is to deny reality itself <p> At this juncture , reform is no longer a luxury , it is an existential necessity . Calls to expand the Security Council , including permanent seats for Africa and Latin America , have gained traction but stalled in endless debate . Proposals for limiting the veto in cases of mass atrocities remain blocked by the very powers that benefit from the status quo . Meanwhile , younger and smaller nations grow impatient , questioning why an institution meant to represent " We the Peoples " should be beholden to a few powerful states . <p> At its 80th anniversary , the UN faces a stark choice , adapt or become irrelevant . This means democratizing the Security Council , strengthening the General Assembly 's role , and investing in preventive diplomacy rather than reactive crisis management . It also means giving civil society , youth , and marginalized voices a genuine seat at the table , not just token participation . <p> The world of 1945 is not the world of 2025 . The situation requires urgent attention from the Borno State Ministry of Agriculture before it escalates into a full-blown disaster . <p> Farmers around Maiduguri have been raising alarms over strange infestations that are destroying maize , millet , sorghum , vegetables , and even newly planted rice fields . These pests and diseases , many of which are unfamiliar to the local farming population , spread rapidly , leaving behind swathes of farmland in ruin . Left unchecked , this problem could wipe out entire harvests and worsen food insecurity in a region already battling humanitarian challenges . <p> For many families in Borno , farming is not just a business -- it is survival . Erratic rainfall patterns and rising temperatures create fertile conditions for pests and diseases to thrive . Farmers who once relied on predictable seasons now find themselves struggling to cope with infestations that emerge unexpectedly . Without adequate agricultural extension support , many of them are left to guess solutions , often relying on ineffective or harmful pesticides . <p> The Borno State Ministry of Agriculture must take leadership In this fight . The first step is deploying agricultural extension officers to affected communities to properly identify the pests and diseases ravaging farmlands . Without accurate diagnosis , any intervention will amount to guesswork . The ministry should collaborate with research institutions , such as the Lake Chad Research Institute , to analyze these outbreaks and recommend scientifically tested @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ support farmers with subsidized pesticides , improved seedlings resistant to pests , and training on integrated pest management . Quick intervention now will save millions of naira in agricultural losses later . <p> Equally important is community awareness . Many farmers are unaware of the best practices to prevent the spread of crop diseases . Simple measures such as crop rotation , timely weeding , and safe pesticide use can make a huge difference . The ministry should organize training sessions and awareness campaigns in local languages to reach grassroots farmers directly . <p> If nothing is done , the consequences will go beyond agriculture . Food insecurity will increase , humanitarian needs will deepen , and rural-urban migration will rise as farmers abandon unproductive lands . Policies and interventions should not be designed from air-conditioned offices alone . The land that fed generations is now barren , and its people scattered . <p> Bultu Briya was not always like this . @@129803057 <p> It is a sobering reality that one South African bank , Standard Bank Group , has a market capitalisation of roughly ZAR 384.34 billion ( about $21-22 billion ) , while the entire Nigerian banking sector combined can not match it . For a nation of more than 200 million people , with an economy that should be the beating heart of Africa , the fact that a single Johannesburg-based bank can outweigh the collective worth of Nigeria 's 33 licensed banks is more than embarrassing ; it is scandalous . <p> This disparity is not just about prestige . It is about the fundamental ability of Nigeria 's banking system to mobilise capital , finance development , and command investor trust . The comparison with South Africa , a country with less than one-third of Nigeria 's population and a smaller GDP in nominal terms , lays bare the structural weaknesses that have crippled Nigerian banks for decades . <p> As of May 2025 , Nigerian banks listed on the Nigerian Exchange ( NGX ) had a combined market capitalisation of about N10.5 trillion . In dollar terms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to less than $8 billion . That is the total value investors are willing to place on the entire Nigerian banking system . By contrast , South Africa 's top six banks together are valued at more than $70 billion . Individually , Standard Bank alone commands a market cap of around $21.8 billion , while FirstRand hovers at about $20.5 billion . Absa , Nedbank , and Investec all sit comfortably in the multi-billion-dollar bracket . In Nigeria , the biggest player , GTCO , is valued at less than $2 billion , barely a fraction of its South African peers . Access Holdings , despite boasting assets above N32 trillion ( $71 billion ) , trades at a market cap of just about $710 million . The disconnect between asset size and market value speaks volumes about investor distrust , weak governance , and systemic fragility . <p> The paradox of Nigeria 's banking industry is that on paper it appears profitable , yet in reality it is fragile . In 2024 , the top five lenders declared after-tax profits that surged more than 270 percent year-on-year . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had evaporated , slowing to a meager 0.74 percent . The supposed windfall profits were largely a mirage created by the naira 's freefall , which inflated the value of foreign currency holdings on paper . These were not profits born of efficiency , innovation , or stronger lending ; they were accounting artifacts . The Central Bank of Nigeria ( CBN ) , seeing the danger , stepped in to block banks from paying out these revaluation gains as dividends , insisting they be held as buffers against future shocks . That intervention exposed the hollowness of the profit 's narrative . <p> The recapitalisation push is the clearest sign yet of the sector 's fragility . With six months to the March 31 , 2026 , deadline , the CBN has confirmed that fourteen banks have so far scaled the recapitalisation hurdle . The contradiction is stark , record profits on one hand , desperate fundraising on the other . <p> The currency crisis further underscores the fragility of Nigeria 's financial system . It is not just a technical matter of exchange rates ; it is a reflection of waning investor confidence , policy inconsistency , and the erosion of the naira 's credibility . And this credibility gap feeds directly into why Nigerian banks are so poorly valued compared to their peers . <p> This is not the first time Nigerian banks have faced such a reckoning . In 2004-2005 , then CBN Governor Charles Soludo spearheaded a bold consolidation exercise that shook the industry to its foundations . At the time , Nigeria had eighty-nine banks , most of them undercapitalised , fragile , and unable to finance large-scale projects . Soludo raised the minimum capital base from N2 billion to N25 billion , forcing mergers and acquisitions that reduced the number of banks to 25 by 2005 . The exercise created bigger , more competitive players like Zenith , GTBank , Access , and UBA , which for a time stood tall on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the wave of oil-driven economic growth , and built reputations as ambitious challengers to South African dominance . <p> But the momentum did not last . The global financial crisis of 2008 , compounded by oil price volatility and weak regulatory oversight , exposed vulnerabilities . Many banks were overexposed to the stock market and the oil sector . By 2009 , a new CBN governor , Sanusi Lamido Sanusi , had to intervene with another round of reforms , including emergency bailouts , leadership changes , and tighter risk management rules . While those measures stabilised the sector , they also clipped its wings , pushing banks towards conservatism rather than innovation . Over the next decade , as South African banks deepened their continental footprint and attracted global investors , Nigerian banks retreated into a survival mode , relying more on government securities , forex arbitrage , and fee-based income than on transformative lending . <p> Today , the consequences are clear . Meanwhile , Standard Bank and FirstRand are rewarded with valuations in the tens of billions because they have built reputations for governance , stability , and consistent growth , even in a difficult South African economy . <p> The implications of this disparity go far beyond balance sheets . Banking is the lifeblood of any economy . Without robust , well-capitalised banks , Nigeria can not fund the infrastructure , industrialisation , and job creation it desperately needs . Instead of driving development , banks have become rent-seekers , charging high fees , exploiting exchange rate gaps , and surviving on government bond yields . This is not banking for growth ; it is banking for survival . The danger is that Nigeria 's banking sector could become increasingly irrelevant on the continental stage . Governance must be overhauled to eliminate opacity , insider abuses , and regulatory capture . Banks must be compelled to shift their focus from government securities and currency speculation to financing manufacturing , SMEs , and infrastructure , which are the engines of real growth .
